whyItMatters: Closest academic work: it names Agent Pay and argues that its spending rules are enforced away from the issuer. RAILS (arXiv 2606.08790) uses a Verifiable Intent chain as evidence in a worked example. No paper gives a security analysis of Agent Pay or Verifiable Intent (as of 2026-10-21).

Names Agent Pay and Verifiable Intent and works an example that uses a Verifiable Intent autonomous-mode chain as authority evidence; it proposes a clearing layer, not a security analysis of Agent Pay.
Mastercard's own description of the Agent Pay Trust Framework and the Agent Pay Ready mark; announced offerings, not a specification.
Formal analysis of EMV, the card protocol family behind the tokens and cryptograms Agent Pay relies on.
Shows how card protocol flaws persist when issuers, networks and merchants each assume someone else checks.
Unpredictable-number weaknesses: a reminder that cryptogram freshness matters for DSRP payloads too.
Cross-brand confusion attacks; relevant where Mastercard and Visa agent tokens travel through the same SPT and edge.
Relay protection in EMV; background for binding a token to an authorized interaction.
An earlier network-run authentication layer and how liability design shaped it; Agent Pay faces the same liability question.
Security analysis of FIDO2, the basis of the passkeys used for Agent Pay consent.
Card network economics and interchange; Mastercard has published no agent-specific interchange or fee so far.
The HTTP Message Signatures draft for automated traffic that Agent Pay's edge verification resembles.
